To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
nonlinear inhibition enables parallel max-finding in noisy neural networks, and the resulting architecture reproduces Hick’s law without additional readout stages or adaptive thresholds.
nonlinear neurons can make decisions more rapidly than linear ones and that nonlinear inhibition can make a decision-making network more efficient.

(1) a network of neurons with a particular nonlinear response property (the “nWTA”) achieves the optimal time to choose the best option from a set of N possibilities, (2) the network reproduces Hick’s law without the need for an additional readout or adaptive thresholding, and (3) the nonlinearities required to achieve these properties are found in many neurons.

the fundamental problem of how to make decisions.

we propose an architecture that is capable of performing parallel max-finding and reproduces experimentally-observed features of decision-making, and that the key to this performance is a nonlinear inhibition mechanism that is ubiquitous in the brain.

nonlinear inhibition can enable near-optimal parallel computation, even in the presence of noisy inputs.
